entities.name: St. Stephen's Basilica
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
St Stephen's Basilica (Szent István-bazilika) in Budapest, Hungary, consecrated in 1905 after 54 years of construction (a dome collapse delayed completion by 20 years), is Hungary's largest church and co-equal national cathedral — housing the mummified right hand (the Holy Right, Szentjobb) of Hungary's founding king Stephen I, which has been carried in annual processions since 1083 CE, making it the oldest continuously venerated relic in Central Europe. The basilica's construction coincided with Budapest's unification (1873) and the Austro-Hungarian Compromise (1867), making it a monument to Hungarian national identity.

Construction began in 1851 under architect József Hild, who continued the neoclassical design until the dome collapsed in 1868, requiring complete reconstruction. Architect Miklós Ybl rebuilt the basilica in neo-Renaissance style, with his death delaying completion further. The final architect József Kauser completed the building in 1905. Emperor Franz Joseph I attended the consecration, symbolically linking Hungarian Catholic identity with Austro-Hungarian political union.

The Holy Right — St Stephen's mummified hand, kept in a Byzantine-style reliquary — has been Hungary's most sacred relic since Stephen's canonization in 1083 CE. The August 20 procession on St Stephen's Day (Hungary's national holiday commemorating the founding) carries the relic through Budapest in an elaborate ceremony watched by hundreds of thousands. The basilica's dome (96 meters, matching the Hungarian Parliament Building across the Danube at exactly 96 meters — commemorating the Magyar conquest of 896 CE) creates a deliberate visual symmetry expressing state-church equality in Hungarian national life.
